claims.text: HEA nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability at elevated service temperatures primarily because random near-equiatomic mixing creates lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion.
The initial nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, disordered solid solutions with random elemental mixing.
Two batches can be prepared with identical overall compositions but different degrees of random mixing or elemental ordering.
Post-synthesis annealing will promote partial elemental ordering or phase segregation in the control batch.
The proposed stability mechanism is relevant across catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K.
Random mixing of multiple elements increases lattice distortion.
Random multi-element mixing and lattice distortion enhance cohesive energy.
Lattice distortion creates a kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion and lowers atomic mobility.
The increased entropy of multi-element mixing thermodynamically favors an alloy structure.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
Sluggish diffusion increases resistance to coalescence or irreversible agglomeration.
Lower atomic mobility minimizes the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and coalescence.
Randomly mixed HEA nanoparticles will have lower diffusion and retain a disordered solid-solution structure better than an identically composed, partially ordered batch.
Induced elemental ordering will increase atomic mobility and cause phase segregation or coarsening.
Conventional bimetallic or partially segregated nanoparticles typically have higher diffusion and lower phase stability under comparable thermal conditions.
Full entropy stabilization requires nanoparticles to remain in a near-equiatomic composition and size regime.
At excessively large particle dimensions or sufficiently high temperatures, lattice distortion may cease to control diffusion and other kinetic or thermodynamic factors may dominate.
Interactions with supports can modulate nanoparticle thermal stability.
Failure of the randomly mixed batch to show statistically lower diffusion and better structural retention than the annealed batch would falsify the proposed mechanism.
